title: The leading region of many plasmids is adapted for translational efficiency.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed all five GitHub tables (TableS1 metadata 4,753 rows x 26 cols; TableS2 restriction targets 645x7; TableS3 DefenseFinder 7,004x25; per-gene GC 205,942x2; PTU-MOB map 13x2) and both Zenodo archives (analysis_results.tar.gz 30.4 MB, leading_region_oriented_plasmids_1751.tar.gz 50.1 MB) with curl after the Zenodo API timed out twice. Extracted 1,751 FASTA files (one record each, median 91,019 bp, all headers literally '>test'). Joined the codon adaptation index (CAI) table: 205,763 genes, 0 missing values, 0 duplicate gene IDs, covering exactly the 1,751 plasmids flagged Leading.region.analysis==TRUE across 13 plasmid taxonomic units (PTUs). Counted 4,567 anti-defence gene hits in 1,367 plasmids (12 subtypes), 163,960 eggNOG functional annotations (78.7% carrying a COG category), 35,020 genes at open reading frame (ORF) rank <=20, collection dates 2003-2020 with 420 of 1,751 missing. Reproduced the paper's headline contrast myself: mean CAI 0.354 for anti-defence genes versus 0.280 for the rest.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The filtering cascade (19,017 RefSeq200 plasmids -> 4,753 in the 50 commonest PTUs -> 1,751 with a confident leading region), the prodigal v2.6.3 '-p meta' gene-calling settings, the oriT (origin of transfer) detection procedure, the CONJScan relaxase typing, and the single-stranded promoter claim in the F plasmid. I did not re-run prodigal, so I have not verified that the authors' ORF numbering is reproducible from the shipped FASTA files.

a1_downloadable.note: No login anywhere: GitHub raw files fetched directly (MIT licence), both Zenodo archives downloaded in full (CC-BY-SA 4.0). The Zenodo REST API timed out repeatedly but the direct file URLs worked with curl.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the proposed target - does a gene sit in the leading region - the ORF rank counted from the transfer origin is the integer suffix of every gene_id in cai_results_prodigal_meta.tsv (plasmids were re-oriented to start at the leading region), so the label is parsed from one column, not inferred across sources. I verified the parse on all 205,763 rows.

a3_inputs_present.note: Nucleotide sequence for all 1,751 plasmids is present (verified: 1,751 FASTA files, 174 MB extracted, no accession lookups needed). Per-gene protein sequences are NOT shipped; they must be regenerated by running prodigal, one tool on local files, which is effort rather than a lookup problem.

a4_units_stated.note: All quantities are dimensionless and defined in the methods: CAI on 0-1 (verified range 0.102-0.705), GC content as a fraction, palindrome density per 1 kb window, position as an integer ORF rank. No mixed-unit risk.

a5_enough_rows.note: 205,763 labelled gene rows over 1,751 plasmids; 35,020 at ORF rank <=20; 4,567 anti-defence genes. Effective independent units are smaller - 13 PTUs and a few thousand protein families after clustering - but still far above the threshold.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Everything loads in pandas in seconds; the only heavy step is computing protein language model embeddings, which is avoidable by subsampling to ~50,000 proteins on CPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Exact match: the paper claims 1,751 conjugative plasmids in 13 PTUs; TableS1 has exactly 1,751 rows flagged TRUE spanning 13 PTUs, Zenodo ships exactly 1,751 FASTA files, and the CAI table covers exactly those same 1,751 accessions.

a8_label_provenance.note: Position is an observed coordinate, so it passes. But two other candidate labels in this dataset fail outright and must not be used: CAI is computed deterministically from the same codons a sequence model would read (leakage by construction), and the anti-defence calls come from DefenseFinder's profile hidden Markov models, i.e. another tool's output.

B1.why: Five files joining on plasmid accession plus ORF rank; I ran the join and all 205,763 genes matched the 1,751 plasmids.

B2.why: Every csv/tsv parsed first try in pandas; only quirks are a mixed-type Date column and identical '>test' FASTA headers.

B3.why: One pipeline computed every value (one CAI weight table per host, one Rust tool for GC); already normalised by the authors.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values; 0 missing CAI values in 205,763 rows, checked directly.

B5.why: 0 duplicate gene IDs, but near-identical plasmids recur within PTUs (892 Escherichia plasmids), needing clustering.

B6.why: TableS1 columns self-explanatory; nothing documents that the CAI gene_id suffix is rank from the transfer origin.

C1.why: Does leading-region character transfer to unseen gene families and PTUs? A negative result is itself informative.

C2.why: No model for leading-region position, but DefensePredictor and four anti-CRISPR predictors cover the adjacent discovery task, openly.

C3.why: These 205,763 transfer-origin-oriented genes have never been used for machine learning; clear novel/unique-application angle.

C4.why: Annotation itself is minutes of hidden Markov model search; what is slow is wet-lab testing of each candidate anti-defence gene.

C5.why: Dummy baselines obvious (17.0% base rate at rank <=20) and I already reproduced the paper's CAI gap, 0.354 versus 0.280.

D1.why: ESM-2 (open-weight protein language model) fits the regenerated proteins; Nucleotide Transformer fits the DNA windows.

D2.why: 205,763 proteins is too many for laptop CPU embedding; viable only after subsetting to ~50,000 with the 35M checkpoint.

D3.why: ESM-2 is MIT, analysis code MIT, Zenodo data CC-BY-SA 4.0; share-alike only affects redistributed derivatives.

E1.why: Hold out whole PTUs (PTU column seen in TableS1) plus MMseqs2 protein clusters at 30% identity.

E2.why: 13 PTUs with 35-367 plasmids each, verified in the file, plus thousands of protein clusters to hold out.

E3.why: Majority class and per-PTU positional prior; base rate at ORF rank <=20 is 35,020/205,763 = 17.0%.

E4.why: Nothing is measured twice; the label is a positional convention, so there is no replicate noise floor.

E5.why: Known anti-restriction families (ardA, ardB, klcA, psiB) must rank high, and the 0.354-vs-0.280 CAI gap must reappear.

E6.why: Label shuffling within PTU, random-feature replacement, and a GC-plus-CAI-only ablation are all one-liners here.

E7.why: Three options: the 3,002 TableS1 plasmids excluded from the set, collection dates for 1,331 plasmids, non-Enterobacterales plasmids from PLSDB.

E8.why: I already recomputed the paper's anti-defence CAI elevation from the shipped table; the per-position curves are equally reproducible.

G1.why: INSDC accessions, BioSample, BioProject and TaxId present, but protein IDs are prodigal-local, not UniProt.

G2.why: PLSDB (curated plasmid database, tens of thousands of complete plasmids) joins directly on the INSDC nucleotide accession.

G3.why: Accession-to-PLSDB is one-to-one; protein-level joins to defence catalogues are many-to-many through homology.

G4.why: Asks whether transfer-origin codon adaptation holds beyond Enterobacterales and finds anti-defence genes where no profile exists.

H1.why: Both classes present by construction: 35,020 genes near the transfer origin versus 170,743 elsewhere; 4,567 anti-defence versus the rest.

H2.why: Verified in the file: 1,736 of 1,751 plasmids are Enterobacterales, 892 Escherichia, 13 PTUs, one RefSeq snapshot.

H3.why: Honest claim stated precisely in one sentence, with the Enterobacterales and oriT-requirement caveats named.

H4.why: The paper spells out the whole filtering cascade and the Enterobacterales restriction (99.1%) in the methods.

I1.why: Named: Dimitriu (Exeter), Rocha and Bernheim (Institut Pasteur), de la Cruz (Santander), Shaw (Oxford/Bristol).

I2.why: Would reorder which plasmid genes get cloned for defence-challenge assays, but these labs already use positional enrichment plus profiles.

I3.why: Precision in the top 100 matches the cloning decision, but the training label (position) is a proxy for anti-defence function.

I4.why: The paper's own result means GC plus CAI may already carry most of the positional signal; complexity unproven.

J1.why: Grouped splits, homology clustering, frozen protein language model embeddings, calibration and transfer across PTUs.

J2.why: Plasmid biology needs some intuition; the authors' published figures give a sanity check, but no expert on hand.

J3.why: A tidy 205,763-row gene table (rank, CAI, GC, function, anti-defence flag) is publishable even if the model is mediocre.

J4.why: Three weeks proposed: one for gene calling and the table, one for embeddings, one for grouped evaluation.

J5.why: Kill condition written in this evaluation (two-feature baseline ties the language model) but not yet in NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: DefensePredictor (DeWeirdt et al., Science 2025) - gradient-boosted classifier on ESM-2 protein language model embeddings of a gene plus its two neighbours each side
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on homologs of known defence and non-defence genes in ~17,000 prokaryotic reference genomes; evaluated on five folds split by MMseqs2 homology clusters so homologs stay together, and prospectively recovered 82 of 100 defence systems discovered after training.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalising beyond homologs of known systems, and the fact that in-silico hits still need experimental confirmation, is what they name as the open part.

existing_models.name: Anti-CRISPR protein predictors: AcRanker (XGBoost on amino-acid composition), DeepAcr, AcrNET, PreAcrs, PaCRISPR, collected in the AcrHub database
existing_models.score_and_split: AcrNET reports roughly 15% better F1 than PaCRISPR, AcRanker and DeepAcr in a cross-dataset test; DeepAcr reports 94-96% accuracy on a 15% random hold-out, which is a weak split given the few hundred known positives.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: All of them name the tiny, biased positive set (only experimentally confirmed anti-CRISPRs) and poor transfer to new phage/plasmid families.

existing_models.name: Plasmid host-range predictors: PlasmidHostFinder (random forest on 8-mers), HOTSPOT (transformer over protein tokens), MOSTPLAS, HRPredict
existing_models.score_and_split: PlasmidHostFinder reports Matthews correlation 0.662-0.867 from species to order level; HOTSPOT predicts phylum to species. Different task (host, not gene position), listed because they are the only published models trained on this exact data type.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Broad-host-range plasmids and under-sampled taxa are named as the hard cases.

existing_models.name: AntiDefenseFinder / DefenseFinder (Tesson, Bernheim and colleagues) - 156 anti-defence systems as profile hidden Markov models, not machine learning
existing_models.score_and_split: No held-out performance number: it is a curated homology search, and it produced the 4,567 anti-defence labels I counted in this very dataset.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: They state that systems with no known homolog are invisible to profile search, which is precisely the gap a learned model could fill.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model), small checkpoints esm2_t12_35M or esm2_t30_150M; Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 as a DNA-side alternative
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU, 16 GB RAM, after subsetting to ~50,000 proteins; embeddings cached once to disk
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT; the data is MIT (code repository) and CC-BY-SA 4.0 (Zenodo)

integration.partner_dataset: PLSDB, the curated database of complete plasmid sequences (tens of thousands of entries), plus DefenseFinder/AntiDefenseFinder's anti-defence catalogue
integration.join_key: INSDC nucleotide accession for plasmids (present and verified in TableS1); protein sequence via MMseqs2 for the defence catalogue
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does the codon adaptation peak at the plasmid transfer origin hold across the whole plasmid universe rather than just Enterobacterales, and can a model trained on position flag anti-defence genes in clades where no profile hidden Markov model exists?

controls.positive_control: The model must rank the known anti-restriction families (ardA, ardB, klcA, psiB) near the top, and the pipeline must reproduce the CAI gap I measured (0.354 for anti-defence genes versus 0.280 for the rest).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the position label within each PTU and confirm collapse to the 17.0% base rate; replace features with random noise; ablate to GC plus CAI alone to see how much of the signal is two numbers.
controls.external_validation: The 3,002 TableS1 plasmids excluded from the leading-region set, a temporal split on collection date (2003-2020, present for 1,331 of 1,751 plasmids), and non-Enterobacterales plasmids pulled from PLSDB.

honest_claim_h3: Among complete, transfer-origin-bearing conjugative plasmids from Enterobacterales in RefSeq (99.1% of this set, 51% from Escherichia), a gene's own sequence predicts whether it lies in the first ~20 open reading frames after the transfer origin, including for gene families held out of training.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a plasmid gene's sequence to predict whether it sits in the leading region, the first DNA to enter a new host cell.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is one plasmid gene: its DNA and protein sequence, its codon adaptation score and GC content. There are 205,763 genes from 1,751 conjugative plasmids, a count I verified in the downloaded table.
plain_idea.predict: A score for whether the gene lies in the first ~20 genes after the transfer origin. The true answer comes from the position of the gene in plasmids that the authors re-oriented to begin at the transfer origin, which they located by matching experimentally confirmed transfer-origin sequences.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs that hunt for genes which help plasmids evade bacterial immune systems currently find them by looking at where they sit in the plasmid; a sequence-only score would let them rank genes in plasmids whose transfer origin is unknown. Even a failure tells us the leading-region signal is family identity rather than transferable sequence character.

more_or_better_data.why: No existing model has seen 205,763 plasmid genes labelled by rank from the transfer origin, which is unique to this release. But DefensePredictor trained on ~17,000 whole genomes, far more sequence than this, for the closely related defence-gene label.

confidence_score.why: Nothing here is measured twice, so there is no replicate-based uncertainty; and DefensePredictor already outputs a per-protein probability, so calibration would not be a new offering.

models_beatable.why: DefensePredictor is 2025, ESM-2-based, split by MMseqs2 homology clusters and tested prospectively on 100 later-discovered systems - an honest evaluation. The anti-CRISPR tools use weak random splits and tiny positive sets, so only they are beatable, and only on their own narrow target.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The label differs: DefensePredictor predicts defence-gene identity, we would predict position relative to the transfer origin, so it cannot be run as a same-label baseline on the same split. The condition that our model sees everything theirs sees plus more fails.

label_elsewhere.sources: Anti-defence gene identity is catalogued across prokaryotes and mobile elements by AntiDefenseFinder/DefenseFinder and, for anti-CRISPRs only, by Anti-CRISPRdb and AcrHub (known resources, confirmed by search). Rank from the transfer origin itself is recomputable for any plasmid with a located transfer origin, for example across PLSDB.
label_elsewhere.join_key: INSDC nucleotide accession for plasmids; protein sequence (MMseqs2 clusters) for gene-level labels
label_elsewhere.why: It means a model trained here can be tested on plasmids from other bacterial orders, which is the only way to know whether the signal is Enterobacterales-specific.

risks: Plasmids within a plasmid taxonomic unit are near-identical backbones - 892 of 1,751 come from Escherichia - so the same gene can appear in both training and test sets.
A handful of anti-defence families (ardA, ardB, klcA, psiB) recur in hundreds of plasmids, letting the model memorise families instead of learning position.
The codon adaptation index is computed with a weight table specific to the host genus, so using it as a feature quietly injects host identity, which correlates with plasmid taxonomic unit.
eggNOG and DefenseFinder columns are homology calls, so using them as features re-injects exactly the family identity the split is trying to hold out.
Using codon adaptation as the label rather than a feature would be pure leakage: it is arithmetic on the same codons the model reads.
leakage_plan.split: Nested hold-out: whole plasmid taxonomic units (the PTU column, which I saw in TableS1, 13 groups of 35-367 plasmids) crossed with MMseqs2 protein clusters at 30% identity (a column that does not exist yet and must be built from the regenerated proteins).
checks: Shuffle the position label within each plasmid taxonomic unit and confirm performance falls to the 17.0% base rate.
Report the nearest-neighbour sequence identity between every test protein and the training set, and recompute scores after dropping test proteins above 40% identity.
Train on codon adaptation plus GC content alone; if those two numbers match the language model, the extra machinery adds nothing.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable, but a serious risk if ignored: with 892 Escherichia plasmids and recurring anti-defence families, a naive random split would produce a flattering and meaningless number.

success_criteria.metric: Precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) for 'gene is within the first 20 open reading frames after the transfer origin', evaluated on held-out plasmid taxonomic units with held-out protein clusters, plus precision among the top 100 ranked genes, because the user will clone roughly 100 candidates.
success_criteria.baselines: Base rate 0.170 (35,020 of 205,763 genes at rank <=20, counted by me); a per-plasmid-taxonomic-unit positional prior; and a logistic regression on codon adaptation plus GC content alone, which should already be strong given the paper's own finding and the gap I reproduced (0.354 versus 0.280).
success_criteria.success: PR-AUC >= 0.34 (twice the 0.170 base rate) on held-out plasmid taxonomic units with protein clusters held out, beating the two-feature codon-plus-GC logistic regression by at least 0.05, with at least three known anti-restriction families appearing in the top 100.
success_criteria.kill: If the codon-adaptation-plus-GC logistic regression comes within 0.02 PR-AUC of the protein language model on held-out plasmid taxonomic units after one week, stop: the paper's own statistic already captures the signal.

ambitious.why: Publishes biology-first machine learning on mobile genetic elements, but would need a predicted anti-defence candidate confirmed in a collaborator's conjugation or restriction assay, not just a held-out score.

realistic.why: Publishes focused predictors and re-analyses of genomic resources; a transfer-origin-position predictor with honest plasmid-taxonomic-unit and homology-cluster splits, plus a candidate list, fits exactly.

fallback.journal: Bioinformatics (Application Note) or a bioRxiv preprint plus the tidy gene table
fallback.why: Even the negative outcome - that two composition features match a protein language model, so leading-region character is family identity - is a publishable short note alongside the released 205,763-gene table.

pitch.headline: 1,751 plasmids re-oriented so each of 205,763 genes carries its rank from the DNA transfer start point, with codon scores attached.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Position is measured from the conjugative transfer origin rather than an arbitrary genome start - 4,567 anti-defence genes flagged, 174 MB of sequence, CC-BY-SA, and every count matching the paper (1,751 of 1,751), all opened and checked.
pitch.the_win: PR-AUC above 0.34 for leading-region membership on held-out plasmid taxonomic units, beating a two-feature GC-plus-codon baseline by 0.05, with ardA, ardB and klcA in the top 100 ranked genes.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn that leading-region character is gene-family memorisation rather than transferable sequence signal, which bounds how far positional enrichment can be pushed as a discovery heuristic.
pitch.who_wants_it: Dimitriu (Exeter) and Rocha/Bernheim (Institut Pasteur), who decide which plasmid genes to clone into restriction and CRISPR challenge assays.

ml_idea: Regenerate open reading frames from the 1,751 re-oriented plasmid FASTA files with prodigal, embed each protein with a frozen small ESM-2 checkpoint, and train a light head to predict whether the gene lies in the first ~20 open reading frames after the transfer origin. Evaluate with plasmid taxonomic units and 30%-identity protein clusters both held out, then use the score to rank the ~42,000 genes with no eggNOG annotation as candidate anti-defence genes. Codon adaptation and GC content are features and the two-feature baseline, never the label.

effort.compute_note: Table sizes and row counts are measured (I parsed every file); the 6-hour embedding figure is an estimate for ~50,000 proteins through esm2_t12_35M on a laptop CPU at roughly 2-3 proteins per second, not timed. Prodigal on 1,751 plasmids of median 91 kb should take well under an hour.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Re-run prodigal v2.6.3 with '-p meta' on 20 of the 1,751 FASTA files and check the per-plasmid gene count against the codon adaptation table (median 104 genes per plasmid, minimum 40). If the open reading frame numbering shifts, the anti-defence and eggNOG label joins are unusable and only the self-computed positional label survives.

verdict_reason: Everything downloads without a login and the counts match the paper exactly (1,751 plasmids, 205,763 genes, 4,567 anti-defence hits, all verified by me), and nobody has trained a model on transfer-origin-oriented plasmid genes. But every label in the release is derived rather than measured: codon adaptation is arithmetic on the same codons a model would read, so it fails the label-provenance killer outright, and the anti-defence calls are profile hidden Markov model outputs. That leaves open reading frame rank from the transfer origin as the only observed target - a proxy whose practical payoff (new anti-defence candidates) is already partly served by the open, honestly evaluated DefensePredictor, and whose coverage is 99.1% one bacterial order with 51% Escherichia. Worth keeping on the shelf, not worth starting this month.
